explain.say: Electricity demand follows our daily routine. It is lowest in the small hours of the night, when most people are asleep and only fridges, street lights and night-shift factories are running.

faq.q: Why is demand lowest at night?
faq.a: Most people are asleep and offices are closed, so only things like fridges, freezers, street lights and some factories keep running. Cheaper night tariffs help fill this trough with electric car charging.
asks: Why is electricity cheaper at night?

faq.q: Why is demand highest in the early evening?
faq.a: In the early evening homes are busy with cooking, lighting, TV and heating, while some workplaces are still open. In Britain the peak is usually on dark winter weekday evenings, around 5 to 7 pm.
asks: What time is peak electricity demand?

faq.a: It is the shape of the demand left for power stations on a sunny day where lots of solar is installed. Solar pushes midday demand down like a duck's belly, then demand shoots up as the sun sets, like its neck.
asks: Why does solar change the demand curve?

faq.q: Why does the morning rise matter?
faq.a: Demand can climb by many gigawatts in a couple of hours as the country wakes up, so control rooms must bring extra power stations online in time.
asks: How fast does demand rise in the morning?

faq.q: How do controllers know what demand will be?
faq.a: They forecast it from the weather, time of year, day of the week and even the TV schedule, using years of past data. Small errors are covered by reserve power stations and batteries.

facts: Britain's electricity demand is typically highest on winter weekday evenings.
The duck curve was named by California's grid operator around 2013.

quiz.say: Why does demand on power stations dip at midday in places with many rooftop solar panels?

options.show: Solar panels supply much of the midday need
options.say: Solar panels supply much of the midday need

options.show: People stop using electricity at lunchtime
options.say: People stop using electricity at lunchtime

quiz.why: Rooftop solar covers part of the demand at midday, so less is needed from power stations.

wrong.1: People keep using electricity at midday; solar is simply supplying it.
wrong.2: Power stations do not take lunch breaks; they follow demand.
